```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5, fig.align = "center",
                      dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

In "vibe coding" a programmer describes what the software should do and an
AI coding agent writes, runs and repairs the code. Programming becomes a
sequence of requests, specifications, checks and complaints addressed to
the agent, interleaved with the agent's plans, actions, questions and
reports. How programmers seek help in this setting, and how the agent's
moves shape what they do next, is a question about the process of the
interaction: it concerns which moves follow which, within and across the
two actors. Rinja et al. (2027) studied help-seeking in student-AI
programming interactions from this perspective with heterogeneous
transition network analysis.

This case study follows that line of analysis on the bundled sessions. It
asks how the programmers distribute their moves, how the agent responds to
each kind of request, which agent moves are followed by frustration, what
turn-taking patterns recur, and whether the conclusions are stable. It does
not reproduce the published study and its numbers.

```{r package}
library(htna)
```

## Data

`human_ai` holds 19,347 coded events from 429 vibe-coding sessions. Each
code belongs to one actor, as recorded in the codebook `human_ai_codebook`.

- **Session and order:** `session_id`, `order_in_session`.
- **Human codes:** `Specify`, `Request` (merging the original codes
  Command and Request), `Check` (Correct and Verify), `Inquire`, `Refine`
  and `Frustrate` (Frustrate and Interrupt).
- **AI codes:** `Plan`, `Execute`, `Ask` (merging Ask, Investigate and
  Inquire), `Report` (Explain and Report), `Repair` and `Delegate`.

```{r codebook}
human_ai_codebook
```

The network is built from the data and the codebook, which assigns each
code to its actor.

```{r build}
net <- build_htna(human_ai, node_groups = human_ai_codebook)
```

## How the actors divide their activity

```{r frequencies}
frequencies_htna(net)
```

The programmers' moves are mostly directive: `Request` (29% of their events)
and `Specify` (27%) together make up more than half of them, `Frustrate`
follows with 17%, and questions (`Inquire`, 8%) are rare. The agent mostly
executes (38% of its events), asks (28%) and plans (19%); it seldom repairs
(3%) or delegates (3%). Help is sought by directing the agent rather than by
asking it.

## How the agent responds to each request

The two-step paths from a human code to an AI code show how the agent
responds; lift compares each count with the count expected if the two codes
followed each other at random.

```{r human-to-ai}
print(extract_meta_paths(net, schema = "Human->AI"), n = 8)
```

Requests and specifications are followed by execution (904 and 796 times),
and specifications also often by a question from the agent (784 times,
2.2 times as often as expected). A check is followed by execution 2.5 times
as often as expected: the agent responds to a correction by acting on it.
The agent answers questions (`Inquire`) with both execution and a question
of its own.

## What follows the agent's moves

The reverse paths show what the programmer does after each agent move.

```{r ai-to-human}
print(extract_meta_paths(net, schema = "AI->Human"), n = 8)
```

After an execution the programmer most often issues the next request (921
times, in 269 sessions), and after a plan as well (503). Frustration is the
next most common reaction to an execution (451 times). The schema
`AI->Frustrate` lists every agent move that precedes frustration.

```{r frustration}
extract_meta_paths(net, schema = "AI->Frustrate")
```

Frustration follows a plan 2.22 times as often as expected, more than it
follows an execution (1.50) or a question (1.22), and it rarely follows a
repair (lift 0.46). Programmers react against the agent's plans more than
against its actions.

## Recurring turn-taking

At the level of actor types, four-step meta-paths show how turns are
exchanged.

```{r meta-paths}
extract_meta_paths(net, level = "type", length = 4, min_lift = 1)
```

The most over-represented pattern is AI $\to$ Human $\to$ Human $\to$ AI
(lift 2.07, in 389 of the 429 sessions): the programmer answers an agent
move with two moves of their own before the agent acts again. Patterns
that alternate strictly between the actors follow (lifts 1.81 and 1.63).
Help-seeking in these sessions is a dialogue of short turns in which the
programmer often needs more than one move to redirect the agent.

The paths that start with a question show what a programmer's question
leads to.

```{r inquire}
print(extract_meta_paths(net, schema = "Inquire->AI->Human"), n = 6)
```

A question answered by an execution is most often followed by a new
request (73 times), but a question answered by an execution is also
followed by a further question 6.94 times as often as expected, and a
question answered by a report by a request 7.55 times as often: answers
lead to more questions or to new instructions, in loops.

## Which codes broker the interaction

```{r centralities}
centralities_htna(net, measures = c("InStrength", "Betweenness"))
```

`Execute` receives the most transition weight (in-strength 2.03) and lies
on the most shortest paths (betweenness 29), followed by the agent's `Plan`
(25) and the programmer's `Request` (19). The interaction is held together
by the request-plan-execute cycle.

```{r edge-betweenness, fig.height = 6}
plot_edge_betweenness_htna(net)
```

## Are the conclusions stable?

The bootstrap identifies the transitions that the resampled sessions
reproduce, and pruning with it keeps only those.

```{r bootstrap}
boot <- bootstrap_htna(net, iter = 200, seed = 1)
pruned <- prune_htna(net, method = "bootstrap", boot = boot)
as.data.frame(summary(pruned), what = "actor_pairs")
```

Sixty-eight edges are retained. The AI-to-human block keeps the most (22),
so the responses of the programmers to the agent are the best-supported
part of the network.

```{r pruned-plot, fig.height = 6}
plot_htna(pruned)
```

Case-dropping asks whether the edge weights hold when sessions are removed.

```{r casedrop}
casedrop_reliability_htna(net, iter = 100, seed = 1)
```

The edge weights keep a rank correlation above 0.7 until 90% of the
sessions are dropped (CS coefficient 0.90), so the transition structure
described above is not carried by a few sessions.

## Conclusion

Programmers in these sessions sought help by directing the agent:
requests and specifications dominate their moves, and questions are rare.
The agent answers requests and checks by executing, and the programmers
answer executions and plans with further requests or with frustration,
the latter most often after a plan. The exchange runs in short turns, with
the programmer often making two moves before the agent acts again, and the
structure is stable under resampling and case-dropping.

## References

Rinja, D., Oliveira, E. A., López-Pernas, S., Saqr, M., Specht, M., &
Misiejuk, K. (2027). Unpacking vibe coding: Help-seeking processes in
student-AI interactions while programming. In *Artificial Intelligence in
Education: 27th International Conference, AIED 2026*. Springer Nature
Switzerland. <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-29763-1_35>
